claims.text: Reactive processing such as internal oxidation can produce a controlled, uniformly distributed nanoscale refractory-oxide dispersion in a refractory high-entropy alloy.
Uniformly distributed nanoscale oxide precipitates act as barriers to dislocation motion.
Uniformly distributed nanoscale oxide precipitates inhibit grain-boundary sliding.
The oxide particles stabilize the alloy microstructure at high temperature.
Impeded dislocation motion and microstructural stabilization provide dispersion strengthening and increase creep resistance.
A small volume fraction of nanoscale oxide particles will not significantly increase the alloy's density.
A small volume fraction of nanoscale oxide particles will not significantly interfere with room-temperature strengthening mechanisms.

Relative to an otherwise relevant refractory HEA without oxide dispersion, the modified alloy will exhibit at least a 25% improvement in creep resistance at approximately 1000 degrees Celsius under sustained loading.
Room-temperature tensile properties of the oxide-dispersed alloy will differ from those of the control by less than 5%.
The oxide dispersion will cause no appreciable increase in overall alloy density.
The expected benefit depends on retaining nanoscale oxide dimensions and an optimal oxide volume fraction.
Excessive oxide content or oxide coarsening may embrittle the alloy.
Excessive oxide content or oxide coarsening may increase density enough to compromise the intervention's benefits.
